faq.a: Alcohol causes mitochondrial injury, releasing more AST; the AST/ALT ratio >2 is typical.
faq.q: Why is AST often higher than ALT in alcoholic liver disease?

faq.a: Yes; early fibrosis or compensated cirrhosis may have normal bilirubin but abnormal INR or platelet count.
faq.q: Can a patient with normal bilirubin still have serious liver disease?

faq.a: When the cause remains unclear after serology and imaging, or to stage fibrosis when non‑invasive tools are unavailable.

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with jaundice, ascites and INR 1.8 – what is the next immediate management step? — Assess for encephalopathy, start lactulose, and arrange urgent referral for possible variceal bleed control.
How does the AST/ALT ratio help differentiate alcoholic hepatitis from viral hepatitis? — Ratio >2 suggests alcohol; viral hepatitis usually has ALT > AST.

A patient with known HBV presents with rising bilirubin but normal ALT – what does this indicate? — Likely progression to cholestatic or decompensated disease; evaluate for biliary obstruction or fibrosis.
Why is spironolactone preferred over furosemide alone for ascites in cirrhosis? — It antagonises aldosterone‑mediated sodium retention, reducing ascites more effectively and sparing potassium.
What red‑flag laboratory finding mandates admission in a patient with chronic liver disease? — INR >1.5 or bilirubin >5 mg/dL indicating impaired synthetic function.

Explain why traditional herbal remedies can precipitate acute liver failure in East Africa. — Many contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids causing hepatocellular necrosis; they are often taken without monitoring.
When is praziquantel indicated in a patient with liver disease? — When schistosomiasis is confirmed or strongly suspected, especially with periportal fibrosis.

How would you differentiate hepatic from cardiac causes of ascites on bedside exam? — Hepatic ascites shows a fluid wave and shifting dullness; cardiac ascites often accompanies jugular venous distension and peripheral edema.
ai.title: Liver Disease
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Liver disease encompasses acute and chronic disorders that impair hepatic function. In low‑resource settings, common causes include viral hepatitis, alcohol, schistosomiasis and drug‑induced injury. Recognising patterns, staging severity, and using limited investigations guide management.

b: Elevated AST/ALT >2 × ULN suggests hepatocellular injury.
Elevated ALP and GGT with bilirubin points to cholestasis.
Ultrasound can detect fatty infiltration, fibrosis or masses.
sections.p: Liver disease refers to any condition that disrupts normal hepatic architecture or function, diagnosed by clinical features, biochemical abnormalities and imaging when available.

b: Child‑Pugh A: compensated, low 1‑year mortality.
Child‑Pugh C: decompensated, high short‑term mortality.
sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical decompensation and fibrosis stage. The Child‑Pugh score (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy) classifies chronic disease into A‑C.

b: Viral hepatitis B and C (endemic, often asymptomatic).
Alcoholic liver injury (common in urban areas).
Schistosoma mansoni hepatic fibrosis (rural exposure).
Aflatoxin‑related hepatocellular carcinoma.
Drug‑induced injury (traditional herbs, anti‑TB drugs).
Non‑alcoholic fatty liver disease (rising with urbanisation).
sections.p: Identify the aetiology to target therapy. In East Africa the hierarchy is:

b: Jaundice, dark urine, pale stools.
Right upper quadrant discomfort or hepatomegaly.
Ascites, peripheral edema, spider angiomas.
Encephalopathy: asterixis, altered mental status.
sections.p: Presentation varies from silent enzyme rise to overt liver failure.
Use tests that answer specific clinical questions; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is there hepatocellular injury? – Marked rise (>5 × ULN) suggests acute hepatitis or toxin exposure.
Is cholestasis present? – Predominant ALP rise indicates biliary obstruction or infiltrative disease.
How severe is jaundice? – Direct >2 mg/dL signals conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
Is synthetic function impaired? – INR >1.5 indicates reduced clotting factor production.
What is the liver’s morphology? – Shows fatty change, fibrosis, masses or biliary dilatation.
Is viral hepatitis the cause? – Positive HBsAg or anti‑HCV confirms infection.

t.a: Schistosoma serology or stool ova exam
t.b: Is schistosomiasis contributing? – Positive test supports hepatic fibrosis from S. mansoni.
Is there cytopenia from portal hypertension? – Thrombocytopenia (<150 × 10⁹/L) suggests splenic sequestration.

b: New onset encephalopathy or asterixis.
Rapidly rising bilirubin >5 mg/dL.
INR >1.5 without anticoagulation.
Severe ascites with tense abdomen.
Upper GI bleed from varices.
sections.p: Identify features that herald rapid deterioration.

b: Antiviral therapy for HBV (tenofovir) or HCV (direct‑acting agents) when available.
Alcohol cessation counseling and withdrawal management.
Praziquantel for active schistosomiasis.
Avoid hepatotoxic drugs (e.g., high‑dose paracetamol, isoniazid without monitoring).
Nutritional support: high‑protein, low‑sodium diet.
Diuretics (spironolactone ± furosemide) for ascites; monitor electrolytes.
Lactulose for encephalopathy; aim for 2–3 soft stools per day.
Beta‑blockers (carvedilol) for variceal bleed prophylaxis if endoscopy unavailable.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, support hepatic function and prevent complications.

b: Every 3–6 months: LFTs, INR, platelets, ultrasound if possible.
Vaccinate against hepatitis A and B for susceptible patients.
Educate on safe herbal use and alcohol moderation.
Screen household contacts for HBV and offer vaccination.
sections.p: Regular monitoring prevents progression and detects complications early.

b: Hemolytic jaundice – indirect bilirubin predominates, normal ALT/AST.
Cardiac cirrhosis (congestive hepatopathy) – history of right‑heart failure, pulsatile liver.
Pancreatic head cancer – obstructive jaundice with weight loss.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic liver disease clinically or biochemically.

b: Mild ALT rise may be absent in chronic hepatitis B; rely on serology.
Normal INR early in acute liver failure; repeat testing is essential.
Ultrasound may miss early fibrosis; clinical scoring (Child‑Pugh) remains vital.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of consciousness or seizures (possible hepatic encephalopathy).
Severe abdominal pain with guarding (possible spontaneous bacterial peritonitis).
